strong_form: Highly agentic or eminent people experienced an early break from normal social embedding (e.g. parental loss, exile, illness, ostracism) at rates well above those of matched non-eminent peers.
weak_form: Early disruption of social belonging is correlated with later independence of mind in some eminent populations.
refuted_if: Matched-cohort data show eminent or high-agency people had early social ruptures at rates no higher than comparable non-eminent controls.

prior_art.citation: Eisenstadt 1978, 'Parental Loss and Genius', American Psychologist (699 eminent persons; high orphanhood rates)
Eugene Wei, 'Eminent orphans' (bereavement also high among less eminent achievers)
Gregory 1965 on whether eminence arises in spite of or because of early adversity
WGBH, 'Successful children who lost a parent: why are there so many of them?'

strongest_criticism: The evidence is mostly historical samples with poor baselines: parental death was common before modern medicine, and delinquents and psychiatric patients show high bereavement too, so the rupture may raise variance rather than agency. 'Break with social reality' is loose enough to fit almost any biography, and 'usually' is not quantified. 'High agency' has no agreed measure.
